title: Resonance Effect — +R and -R
notes: **Definition:** the delocalisation of pi ($\pi$) electrons or lone pairs through a conjugated system of alternating single and multiple bonds, resulting in the transmission of electron density across the molecule. The actual structure is a resonance hybrid — a weighted average of all canonical (resonance) forms. No single canonical form represents the true molecule.

**+R effect (electron-donating resonance effect):** groups possessing lone pairs of electrons donate electron density into the conjugated pi system. Common +R groups in decreasing order of strength: $-O^- > -NH_2 > -NHR > -NR_2 > -OH > -OR > -F > -Cl > -Br > -I$. The key feature is a lone pair on an atom directly attached to the conjugated system. Example: in aniline ($C_6H_5NH_2$), the nitrogen lone pair delocalises into the benzene ring, creating negative charge at ortho and para positions.

**-R effect (electron-withdrawing resonance effect):** groups containing multiple bonds to electronegative atoms withdraw electron density from the conjugated pi system. Common -R groups: $-NO_2 > -CN > -SO_3H > -CHO > -COR > -COOH > -COOR > -CONH_2$. The pi electrons of the substituent are pulled toward the more electronegative atom. Example: in nitrobenzene ($C_6H_5NO_2$), the nitro group withdraws electron density from the ring, creating positive charge at ortho and para positions.

**Resonance structures of the nitrate ion ($NO_3^-$):** three equivalent canonical forms exist, each with one N=O double bond and two N-O single bonds. The actual ion has three identical N-O bonds of equal length (124 pm), intermediate between a single (140 pm) and double (115 pm) bond. The resonance energy is approximately 30 kcal/mol.

**Resonance in the carbonate ion ($CO_3^{2-}$):** three equivalent resonance structures distribute the negative charge equally among all three oxygen atoms, making all C-O bonds equivalent (128 pm). This delocalisation explains the exceptional stability of the carbonate ion.

**Effect on aromatic reactivity:** +R groups activate the benzene ring toward electrophilic aromatic substitution by increasing electron density, especially at ortho and para positions. They are ortho/para directors. Example: phenol undergoes bromination without a catalyst, giving 2,4,6-tribromophenol, because $-OH$ strongly activates the ring via +R. -R groups deactivate the ring and are meta directors. Example: nitrobenzene requires harsh conditions for electrophilic substitution and gives predominantly the meta product.

**Resonance vs inductive effect comparison:** (1) Resonance operates through pi bonds; inductive through sigma bonds. (2) Resonance is stronger and operates over longer distances. (3) Resonance requires a conjugated system; inductive operates in any saturated chain. (4) Resonance can reverse the expected direction of electron flow — in chlorobenzene, chlorine is electronegative (-I) but donates electrons by resonance (+R).

**Benzoquinone resonance:** 1,4-benzoquinone has two major resonance contributors that illustrate how the carbonyl groups withdraw electron density from the ring. The molecule is highly reactive as a dienophile in Diels-Alder reactions because the electron-withdrawing C=O groups make the double bonds electron-poor.

**Mesomeric effect in peptides:** the peptide bond ($-CO-NH-$) exhibits resonance between the carbonyl and amino groups, giving the C-N bond partial double-bond character (1.32 Å vs typical C-N single bond of 1.49 Å). This restricts rotation and creates a planar geometry, which is fundamental to protein secondary structure (alpha helices and beta sheets).

**Real-world application:** the colour of organic dyes and pigments arises from extended conjugated pi systems where resonance delocalisation lowers the energy gap between HOMO and LUMO. For example, beta-carotene (orange in carrots) has 11 conjugated double bonds, and its resonance-stabilised electron system absorbs blue light, reflecting orange. Indigo (blue dye) derives its colour from resonance between two lactam rings connected by a double bond.
confusion: +R vs +I effect — Both donate electrons, but +R works through pi systems via lone pair delocalisation, while +I works through sigma bonds via electronegativity differences. The $-O^-$ group shows the strongest +R effect (lone pair donation), while alkyl groups show +I (sigma electron release). A group cannot show both +R and +I simultaneously in the same direction for the same atom.

Why Cl is ortho/para director despite being deactivating — Chlorine has a strong -I effect (withdraws electrons, deactivating the ring) but also a +R effect (donates lone pairs, directing ortho/para). The -I effect dominates reactivity (making chlorobenzene less reactive than benzene), but the +R effect controls orientation ( directing incoming electrophiles to ortho/para positions).

Resonance hybrid vs equilibrium — Resonance structures are NOT in equilibrium; they are imaginary representations of a single real structure (the hybrid). The molecule does not flip between forms. This is fundamentally different from tautomerism, where actual isomers interconvert. The resonance hybrid of benzene has six equivalent C-C bonds of 139 pm, not alternating single and double bonds.

Order of +R groups — The strength of +R depends on the willingness of the atom to donate its lone pair. More electronegative atoms hold their lone pairs more tightly, reducing their +R effect: $-O^- > -NH_2 > -OH > -F$. The negatively charged oxygen in $-O^-$ is the strongest +R donor because it has both a lone pair and a full negative charge to donate.

-R effect in $-NO_2$ vs $-COOH$ — Both withdraw electrons by resonance, but $-NO_2$ is a stronger -R group because nitrogen can accept electron density into its empty antibonding orbital, whereas in $-COOH$, the carbon already has a full octet. This is why nitrobenzene is far less reactive toward electrophilic substitution than benzoic acid.
practice: Draw all valid resonance structures for the carbonate ion ($CO_3^{2-}$), the nitrate ion ($NO_3^-$), and the allyl cation ($CH_2=CH-CH_2^+$). For each, indicate the movement of electrons using curved arrows and identify which structures are equivalent versus which make the major contribution to the hybrid.

Explain why aniline is activated toward electrophilic substitution while nitrobenzene is deactivated. Draw the resonance structures of aniline showing how the $-NH_2$ group donates electron density to the ring, and draw the resonance structures of nitrobenzene showing how the $-NO_2$ group withdraws electron density.

Predict the orientation (ortho/para vs meta) and activation/deactivation effect of the following substituents on electrophilic aromatic substitution: $-OCH_3$, $-CN$, $-NHCOCH_3$, $-CH_3$, $-SO_3H$. For each, state whether the effect is primarily inductive or resonance-based.

Explain why the C-N bond in the peptide linkage has partial double-bond character. Draw the two resonance structures of the peptide bond and discuss the implications for protein structure, including why proline introduces kinks in polypeptide chains.

Arrange the following in order of increasing acidity and explain using resonance arguments: phenol, $p$-nitrophenol, $p$-methoxyphenol. Consider how each substituent affects the stability of the phenoxide ion through both resonance and inductive effects.
universalFacts: The concept of resonance was introduced by Linus Pauling in the 1930s as part of valence bond theory. It explains why certain molecules have properties that cannot be accounted for by any single Lewis structure.

Resonance energy is the difference in energy between the resonance hybrid and the most stable canonical form. For benzene, the resonance energy is approximately 36 kcal/mol, explaining its exceptional stability and reluctance to undergo addition reactions.

The number of resonance structures correlates with stability: more equivalent resonance structures mean greater delocalisation and higher resonance energy. Ozone ($O_3$) has two equivalent structures; benzene has two equivalent Kekulé structures plus four Dewar structures.

Resonance effects are exploited in drug design — many pharmaceuticals contain aromatic systems with resonance-active substituents that interact with biological targets through pi-stacking and hydrogen bonding.

In molecular orbital theory, resonance is described as the linear combination of atomic orbitals to form delocalised molecular orbitals. The pi electrons in benzene occupy three bonding molecular orbitals that extend over all six carbon atoms.
